In its FY2024 10-K, JPMorganChase disclosed that its Board authorized a new $30 billion common share repurchase program on June 28, 2024, effective July 1, 2024, replacing a prior $30 billion program announced on April 13, 2022 [1]. During 2024, the Firm repurchased 91,719,226 shares at an average price of $205.43 for a total of $18,841 million, leaving $19,326 million remaining at year-end [2]. In its FY2025 10-K, the Board authorized a new $50 billion common share repurchase program effective July 1, 2025, replacing the prior $30 billion authorization that was announced on June 28, 2024 [3]. During 2025, the Firm repurchased shares at an average price of $276.55 for a total of $31,640 million, with $33,423 million remaining under the repurchase program at year-end [4].

Both the FY2024 and FY2025 annual reports refer to Notes 21 and 26 for discussions of restrictions on dividend payments and cross-reference the Capital actions section of MD&A for information on the common dividend payout ratio [1][3]. The FY2024 10-K refers to Note 26 for the amount of dividends JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. could pay at January 1, 2025 to JPMorganChase without banking regulator approval, while the FY2025 10-K provides the equivalent reference as of January 1, 2026 [5][6]. Both filings warn that failure to maintain required capital levels, or any decision to use regulatory buffers allowing capital ratios to decline below regulatory requirements, could constrain the amount of dividends payable on common stock and reduce the amount of common stock the Firm is permitted to repurchase [7][8].

In its FY2024 10-K risk factors, JPMorganChase noted that uncertainty remained regarding the final versions of the 2023 Basel III rule proposal and the 2023 Federal Reserve proposal to amend the GSIB surcharge calculation, and that the final rules could impact the Firm's levels of capital distributions to its shareholders [7]. The FY2024 Item 1 business section stated that "[f]inalization of the proposal, including the required implementation date, is uncertain," while the FY2025 10-K added that in September 2025 the Federal Reserve's Vice Chair for Supervision indicated an updated proposal may be issued in early 2026 to replace the July 2023 proposal [9][10]. On EU Basel III market risk rules, the FY2024 10-K stated they were delayed until January 1, 2026, whereas the FY2025 10-K reflected an updated timeline, noting "market risk aspects expected to be delayed until January 1, 2027 [9][10]."

On stress testing, the FY2024 10-K reported that the Federal Reserve indicated in December 2024 its intent to seek public comment on changes to its stress testing framework, and that a legal challenge to stress testing administration was pending [11]. The FY2025 10-K reported that in October 2025 the Federal Reserve issued two formal proposals to revise the supervisory stress testing framework requiring public comment on models and scenarios, and in February 2026 released final 2026 stress test scenarios while announcing that SCB requirements for large banks, including the Firm, would remain at current levels through September 30, 2027 [12][13]. The FY2025 10-K also disclosed that in April 2025 the Federal Reserve proposed a rule to reduce SCB volatility by averaging the SCB requirement over a two-year period and extending the annual effective date of the SCB by one quarter, though that proposal had not been finalized [13].
